section.title: The Birth of Obed
section.sectionRationale: The final movement resolves and crowns the whole book. Ruth bears a son, the empty Naomi is filled, the women bless the LORD who gave a redeemer, and the closing genealogy quietly reveals the point of it all: this child leads to David. It is one unit that turns a family's rescue into the hinge of Israel's, and the world's, redemptive history.
section.thesis: The LORD who emptied Naomi now fills her arms with a redeeming grandson, and the genealogy pulls back the curtain: the whole story of famine, loyalty, and redemption was God quietly preparing the line of David, and through David the Messiah.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the birth of Obed and the women's blessing of God; Naomi filled with the child on her lap; and the genealogy from Perez to David that discloses God's purpose.

units.label: The birth and the women's blessing

verses.text: So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. And when he had relations with her, the LORD enabled her to conceive, and she gave birth to a son.
Then the women said to Naomi, “Blessed be the LORD, who has not left you this day without a {{goel|kinsman-redeemer}}. May his name become famous in Israel.
He will renew your life and sustain you in your old age. For your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given him birth.”

units.label: Naomi filled
units.note: a son has been born to Naomi

verses.text: And Naomi took the child, placed him on her lap, and became a nurse to him.
The neighbor women said, “A son has been born to Naomi,” and they named him {{obed|Obed}}. He became the father of Jesse, the father of {{david|David}}.
Now these are the {{toledot|generations}} of Perez: Perez was the father of Hezron,
Hezron was the father of Ram, Ram was the father of Amminadab,
Amminadab was the father of Nahshon, Nahshon was the father of Salmon,
Salmon was the father of Boaz, Boaz was the father of Obed,
Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David.

goel.gloss: Kinsman-redeemer or guardian-redeemer, the near relative who rescues his kin and secures the family's future. Strikingly, the women call the newborn child Naomi's goel: the baby Obed secures her line and old age, an heir who redeems her from emptiness. The word crowns the theme that has run through the book and points to Christ, the Redeemer born in this very line.

obed.gloss: Obed, meaning one who serves or worships. The son of Ruth and Boaz is placed on Naomi's lap and named by the neighbor women; he becomes the grandfather of David. The empty widow is filled with a servant-son who secures her future and carries the line of promise forward.

david.gloss: David, whose name means beloved, Israel's greatest king. The whole book has been quietly climbing to this name: the story of famine, loyalty, and redemption was God's way of preparing the royal line. Beyond David stands the Messiah, great David's greater Son, Jesus, Matthew 1:1 and 1:5-6.

toledot.gloss: Generations, or an account of descendants. The same genealogical formula that structures the book of Genesis closes Ruth, tying this small, tender story into the great line of promise. Matthew 1 takes up these very names, placing Ruth and Boaz in the ancestry of Jesus the Messiah.

basic.context: Boaz marries Ruth, and God gives them a son. The women of Bethlehem bless the LORD and tell Naomi that this child is her redeemer, who will renew her life; they even say Ruth, who loves her, is better than seven sons. Naomi, once empty, now holds a grandson on her lap. The book ends with a short family tree revealing that this baby, Obed, is the grandfather of King David.
basic.hermeneutics: This ending reframes the whole book. What seemed a private tale of grief and rescue turns out to be a chapter in God's public plan for Israel and the world. The genealogy is not a dull appendix but the punchline: God was building the royal line all along. Naomi's fullness answers her emptiness in chapter one, closing the story's great reversal.
basic.originalLanguages: The women call the baby a goel, a redeemer, for Naomi, showing the child secures her future. He is named Obed, one who serves. The closing toledot, the account of generations, links Ruth to the great line, and the final word of the book is David, the name the whole story was quietly building toward.
basic.typology: Obed the redeemer-child who fills the empty and renews Naomi's life points to Christ, the child born to redeem and to give life. The line to David is the line to great David's greater Son. Ruth, an outsider in the Messiah's family tree, foreshadows the nations gathered into Christ.
basic.christ: The book ends by naming David, and the New Testament finishes the line: from David comes Jesus, Matthew 1. Ruth and Boaz are Christ's ancestors, and their story of redemption was God's quiet preparation for the great Redeemer. The child who renewed Naomi's life points to the Child who brings resurrection life to all His people.
basic.god: God, who seemed hidden through the whole book, is openly praised at the end: it is the LORD who gave conception and the redeemer. We learn that God fills the empty, that He weaves private sorrows into His public plan of salvation, and that His providence was steering every step toward the King and the Messiah.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 16 anoints David from this line. Matthew 1 carries it to Jesus. And Naomi's fullness echoes the God who lifts the poor and fills the hungry in 1 Samuel 2 and Luke 1.
basic.oneStory: The whole story lands here: the emptied widow is filled, and the child in her lap leads to David and to Jesus. Ruth's small story of loyalty and redemption turns out to be a vital link in the one great story of God redeeming a people and sending the King, the true Redeemer, born in Bethlehem.

context.literary:
The unit closes the book by shifting genre twice within ten verses: warm, personal narrative in verses 13 to 17 gives way to the spare, formulaic list of verses 18 to 22, a deliberate change of register that signals the story is now stepping back from Bethlehem's streets to view the whole family from a national height. The book that opened, in the days when the judges ruled, 1:1, closes on the name of the king whose reign will end that era, so that the entire span of Ruth answers a question its very first line quietly raises.

Naomi's action in verse 16, taking the child and placing him on her lap, echoes a recognized ancient gesture of legitimation found elsewhere in Genesis, where Jacob formally reckons his grandsons Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons before blessing them at his knees, Genesis 48:5-12, and where Joseph's own great grandsons are later described as being brought up on Joseph's knees, Genesis 50:23. The neighbor women's declaration, a son has been born to Naomi, verse 17, completes the gesture in words: legally and socially, this child answers Naomi's own line, even though Ruth bore him, showing how ancient family structures could fold a daughter-in-law's child fully into a mother-in-law's house.

The chapter's earlier bitterness in Naomi's own mouth, call me Mara, for the Almighty has made my life very bitter, 1:20, is never directly answered by a change of name here; instead the narrator lets the reversal of her circumstances, empty hands become a full lap, argue louder than any renaming could. And the genealogy's plain, unadorned form deliberately echoes the toledot formula that structures Genesis, binding this small family record to the same literary tradition that carries Israel's whole origin story.
context.historical:
That the neighbor women, rather than Ruth or Boaz, are the ones who name the child is a small but telling social detail; it shows a community claiming a stake in this birth, treating Obed as answered prayer for the whole town of Bethlehem rather than a private family matter. In a world where a widow's security depended entirely on male relatives, a grandson meant Naomi would not end her days destitute, and the text's note that Naomi became a nurse to him, a term that can describe a wet nurse or a caregiver, shows her taking a full, daily role in his upbringing rather than a merely honorary one.

The closing genealogy also follows a recognizable and deliberate shape. Genesis structures its earliest history around exactly ten generation lists, Adam to Noah, Genesis 5, and Shem to Abram, Genesis 11:10-26, and Ruth's genealogy from Perez to David likewise runs exactly ten names, an editorial choice that ties this family record to Israel's oldest and most authoritative genealogical form rather than to a looser, ordinary family tree. An audience steeped in Genesis would have recognized the pattern immediately and understood that the author was claiming the same kind of foundational significance for this list that Genesis claimed for its own.

Historically, this closing genealogy would have carried real weight for a monarchy that needed its founding king's ancestry beyond dispute; tracing David cleanly from Judah's son Perez through a documented, witnessed redemption answered any question about the legitimacy of Israel's royal house, at a time when surrounding nations regularly justified their kings by manufactured or disputed genealogies of their own.
context.canonical:
This closing genealogy makes Ruth one of only four women singled out by name in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Uriah, Matthew 1:3-6, each of them an outsider or a woman whose story carried some scandal or risk in Israel's eyes, and each nonetheless woven into the Messiah's own family line without embarrassment. Ruth's inclusion here is therefore not an isolated compliment to one worthy woman; it is part of a pattern the New Testament will later draw attention to on purpose, showing that God's chosen line was never limited to the comfortable or the conventional.

In most Christian orderings of the Old Testament, Ruth sits directly before 1 and 2 Samuel, so that this chapter's final word, David, functions as a literal bridge into the very next book, where the boy Samuel will one day anoint this same shepherd king, 1 Samuel 16:1-13. The two books share more than a place in the canon; Ruth 4 supplies the ancestry that 1 Samuel's narrative will spend chapters catching up to, so that a reader moving straight through Scripture meets David's name here well before meeting the man himself.

The genealogy is also preserved almost verbatim in 1 Chronicles 2:9-15, written centuries later when Israel, newly returned from exile, needed to reestablish exactly whose descendants could still claim the promises tied to David's house, showing that this quiet ending to a small book kept mattering to Israel's identity long after the events themselves.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The author closes his book by drawing back the curtain on something he has let his hearers only guess at until now: this whole account of famine, loss, gleaning, and a bold night at a threshing floor was never only about one family's survival. He wants his audience to feel the shock of scale, that a joy as small and ordinary as a grandmother nursing a baby is, without any of the participants fully realizing it, God quietly assembling the ancestry of Israel's king. In doing so he teaches his hearers not to measure the size of God's work by the size of the stage it happens on; famine, gleaning, and a private family blessing turn out to matter as much to the nation's future as any battle or coronation recorded elsewhere in Scripture. He is also, quietly, defending David's house: by naming every generation from Perez and showing exactly how the marriage that produced Obed came about, in full view of witnesses and blessed by the whole town, he removes any doubt a critic might raise about the legitimacy of Israel's ruling line.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The specific customs on display here, neighbors naming a child, a grandmother functioning as his caregiver, an heir legally folded into another family's line, belonged to Israel's own social world and are not commanded patterns for families today. What does transfer is the theology beneath the customs: that children are gifts the LORD gives rather than achievements parents produce, that a community has a real, godly stake in the wellbeing of its most vulnerable members, and that God is entirely capable of using ordinary domestic joy, a birth, a name, a grandmother's delight, as the hinge of much larger purposes no one present could yet see. Readers should resist mining the genealogy for hidden numerology or reading Naomi's story as a formula guaranteeing every grieving person a grandson; the passage promises God's faithfulness to His larger plan, not a specific outcome to every personal sorrow.

debates.question: Why does the book end with a genealogy rather than a scene?

views.label: To reveal the book's true purpose
views.case: The genealogy is the point, not an afterthought: it discloses that this whole story of famine, loyalty, and redemption was God quietly building the line of David, giving the private drama national and redemptive significance.

views.label: To anchor Ruth in the covenant line
views.case: By tracing Perez to David, the closing verses tie Ruth and Boaz to Judah's promise and to Israel's greatest king, embedding the story in the ongoing plan of God rather than leaving it a self-contained tale.

debates.bearing: Either way the genealogy lifts the reader's eyes from one family's happy ending to God's grand design, which the New Testament completes in Jesus, the son of David, Matthew 1:1.

debates.question: In what sense is the child Obed called Naomi's redeemer?

views.label: The heir who secures her future
views.case: Obed carries on the family name and inheritance and will care for Naomi in old age, redeeming her from the emptiness and vulnerability of chapter one; the women rightly call him her goel.

views.label: A sign of God's redeeming faithfulness
views.case: The child embodies the LORD's covenant kindness to Naomi, the visible proof that God has not left her without a redeemer, so the term points beyond the boy to God's own redeeming work.

debates.bearing: Both senses hold together and point forward: God provides a redeemer to fill the empty, ultimately in Christ, the Redeemer born of this very line.

study.originalLanguages:
The neighbor women give the newborn a title no other child in the Old Testament receives quite this way: they call him a redeemer for Naomi, using the same legal word for kinsman redeemer that has run through the previous two chapters, except that here the redeemer is not a grown man securing land but an infant who simply exists. The extension is deliberate; Obed redeems Naomi's future not by any legal transaction but by being born, showing that redemption in this book has widened from a marriage contract to something closer to pure gift.

A quieter wordplay gathers up the whole book. Naomi's story has been built entirely around forms of the verb shub, to return or turn back: she returns from Moab, 1:6-7, sends her daughters in law to return to their mothers' houses, 1:8, and famously laments that she went away full and the LORD has brought her back, returned her, empty, 1:21. The women's promise in verse 15, that the child will renew her life, turns that same root toward restoration rather than emptiness, so that the very word that once described her bitter homecoming now describes her joy. The book's central verb finally turns all the way around.

The child is named Obed, meaning one who serves or worships, by the neighbor women rather than by his own parents, an unusual detail that shows the whole town, not just one household, claiming a stake in what this birth means. The women also promise the child will sustain Naomi in her old age, using the ordinary Hebrew word for providing and feeding that describes Joseph caring for his starving family, Genesis 45:11, and a foreign widow feeding Elijah, 1 Kings 17:9, quietly placing Naomi's small domestic rescue inside a family of similar stories where God provides for the hungry and the outlived through an unlikely source.

Finally, the closing unit calls itself a toledot, an account of generations, the same word that structures Genesis's ten generation lists, and the verb yalad, to bear or beget, runs through both the personal birth narrative of verse 13 and the formal begettings of verses 18 to 22, binding a mother's labor and a genealogist's record together with the very same word. The list ends, deliberately, on one name, David, the only name in the whole book given no further genealogical successor, leaving the reader's eye fixed there rather than moving on.

typology.type: The child who is himself called a redeemer
typology.fulfillment: No other infant in the Old Testament is named a redeemer; Obed redeems Naomi's future simply by existing, without any transaction or payment on his part. That gift shaped redemption points forward to a Redeemer who likewise saves not by anything He first extracts from those He rescues but by His own arrival among them, God with us, Matthew 1:23. Obed's redemption is limited to one household and one lifetime; the Child later born in the same town redeems every household that will receive Him, and unlike Obed, He chooses and knows the cost of the rescue He becomes.

typology.type: A genealogy that ends deliberately on one unfinished name
typology.fulfillment: Ruth's genealogy stops at David, refusing to run further even though the author certainly knew David's own descendants existed. Matthew's genealogy takes up the unfinished list and carries it all the way to the Christ, Matthew 1:16, showing that Ruth's ending was never a true ending but a pause at the name the whole Old Testament was waiting to hear. The type is one of incompleteness answered by completion: what Ruth leaves open, the Gospel closes.

typology.type: Naomi's emptiness turned to fullness through a given son
typology.fulfillment: Naomi's empty arms are filled by a son given to her, not earned or arranged by her own effort in the end, only received. That shape anticipates the way every sinner receives salvation, empty handed, through a Son given rather than a wage earned, Isaiah 9:6 and Romans 6:23. The escalation lies in the gift's size: Naomi received one grandson to close one family's grief, while those in Christ receive the only Son of God, given once to close humanity's whole exile from Him.

study.christ:
The book ends its account of famine and harvest in a town whose very name, Bethlehem, means house of bread, so that the child born there to end one family's hunger for an heir sits in the same house of bread where, in the fullness of time, the bread of life would be born to end a far deeper hunger, John 6:35. Obed is not merely an ancestor of that later child; his birth in this exact place quietly rehearses the shape of the greater birth to come, unnoticed by empire or history, celebrated only by a small circle of neighbors, exactly as Micah would later promise concerning Bethlehem Ephrathah, small among the clans of Judah, yet the source of the ruler whose origins are from everlasting, Micah 5:2.

The genealogy's inclusion of a Moabite mother matters here as much as its inclusion of David's name. God had promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his line, Genesis 12:3, and this closing list shows that promise already reaching further than ethnic Israel two generations before David is even born; the line that will produce Israel's greatest king already runs, at its root, through a foreign daughter in law who chose Naomi's God as her own. When Matthew later opens his Gospel with this same Ruth in the family tree of Jesus, he is not introducing a surprise; he is finishing a sentence Ruth 4 had already begun.

There is a contrast worth sitting with as well. Naomi receives an heir who will, in time, die like every other child of Adam, useful to her only for the years of her old age. The Son whose birth this genealogy ultimately serves does not merely sustain His people for a season; He is Himself the life that never runs out, able to save completely those who come to God through Him, because He always lives to intercede for them, Hebrews 7:25. Obed filled one grandmother's empty lap for as long as they both lived. Christ fills His people forever.
study.god:
Scripture credits the LORD directly with something wholly ordinary: Boaz and Ruth had relations, as any married couple would, and yet the narrator insists that it was the LORD who enabled her to conceive, verse 13. This is a claim about God's rule over conception as such, not only over famous, miraculous births; the same hand that is elsewhere shown closing and opening wombs by dramatic sign, Genesis 20:18 and 30:22, is here credited just as plainly for a conception that involved no visible wonder at all, teaching that ordinary process and divine gift are never really in competition in Scripture's own account of how life begins.

God also receives praise here through an unusually plain channel: not a prophet, not a psalm, but the spontaneous blessing of the town's women gathered around Naomi. Scripture does not treat their words as a lesser or informal kind of worship; the narrator records their blessing of the LORD with the same seriousness he gives to Eli's priestly blessing back in chapter one, showing that ordinary believers, gathered around an ordinary joy, can speak true theology and real praise without any special office to authorize them.

The chapter's picture of God is finally one of patient, layered provision. He gave bread back to Israel to end the famine, 1:6, gave Ruth favor in Boaz's field, gave Boaz the resolve to redeem, and now gives Naomi a grandson to sustain her, each gift building on the last across years rather than arriving all at once. Nothing here is instantaneous; the God of Ruth works through harvests, seasons, and a nine month pregnancy as comfortably as He works through any single decisive act, and readers who want their prayers answered on a single afternoon might learn from Naomi that the LORD's fullest answers sometimes take a whole book to arrive.

And He is a God who keeps His promises across generations He never announces in advance. Nothing in the earlier chapters told Naomi, Ruth, or Boaz that a king's ancestry was at stake in their small, private decisions; only the closing genealogy shows the reader how far the LORD's hand had actually reached. That hiddenness is itself part of His character here, a God content to work unannounced through famine, gleaning, and a wedding for years before He lets anyone see the shape of what He was building.

crossReferences.note: Naomi once told the women of Bethlehem to call her Mara, bitter, because the LORD had brought her back empty. The very women who heard that lament are the ones who now bless the LORD over her grandson, letting their blessing answer her bitterness without a single word of correction needing to be spoken.

Jacob formally reckons his grandsons Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons and blesses them at his knees, the same gesture behind Naomi taking Obed onto her lap. Both scenes show an older generation legally and physically claiming a grandchild as an heir of their own household.

The genealogy from Shem to Abram runs exactly ten generations, the same length as Ruth's closing list from Perez to David. The repeated form signals that the author wants this family record read with the same weight Genesis gave to the ancestry that produced Abraham himself.

Centuries later the prophet names this same small town as the source of a ruler whose origins are from everlasting, tying Bethlehem's future glory to a lineage this genealogy has already begun to trace from Obed toward David and beyond.

The very next book opens with the LORD sending Samuel to this family's town to anoint a son of Jesse as king, the grandson of the Obed whose birth closes Ruth. The genealogy readers have just finished is the ancestry the following chapters assume without repeating it.

Isaiah later promises a son given whose government and peace will never end. Obed's birth answers one grandmother's need for a lifetime; the Son Isaiah promises answers the world's need forever, and both births are first received as a gift before they are understood as a gift.

Bethlehem's own name means house of bread, and this chapter closes a story that began in famine, 1:1, with a birth in that same house of bread. Centuries later another child born there would call Himself the bread of life, ending a hunger no harvest could satisfy.

Obed could sustain his grandmother only as long as they both lived. The writer to the Hebrews describes a greater Son of this same line who is able to save completely and always lives to intercede, a permanence no human heir, however dear, could ever offer Naomi.

God's promise to Abraham that every family of the earth would be blessed through his line is already advancing in this genealogy, two generations before David is born, through a Moabite daughter in law whose place in Israel's story this chapter makes permanent.

study.oneStory:
This closing scene answers not only Naomi's own grief but the whole book's opening question, what will become of a family that walked out of the promised land during a famine and buried its men in a foreign country. The answer is that death and emigration do not have the final word; the LORD who once let Elimelech's household empty out in Moab now fills Naomi's lap in Bethlehem, and the line that seemed finished continues through exactly the daughter in law many would have expected to be a dead end.

The genealogy quietly gathers up threads reaching back to Eden. The blessing to multiply and fill the earth, Genesis 1:28, keeps meeting resistance across Genesis, barren wives, dead husbands, famine, yet keeps advancing anyway, one more generation at a time, and Ruth's ten names from Perez to David are one more installment in a story of fruitfulness God refuses to let die out, despite every human reason it might have.

The chapter also sits at the exact hinge between Israel without a king and Israel with one. Judges ends with the grim refrain that everyone did what was right in his own eyes; Ruth ends by naming the king who will begin to answer that chaos, even though David himself will not appear in the story's own pages. Between the judges' failure and the king's arrival, God has been working through a family too ordinary for the record books, until the last line surprises the reader with exactly whose ancestor this whole story has been about.

And the same line runs further than the author of Ruth could have known to write. Obed leads to Jesse, Jesse to David, and eventually, through many generations Ruth never lists, to Jesus, the Son of David, who will Himself be born in Bethlehem, welcomed by shepherds rather than a whole town, and who will do for the entire world what Obed's birth did for one grieving grandmother, turn emptiness into everlasting fullness.

sermon.title: The Mystery of History
sermon.why: The closing message of Begg's series A Study in Ruth, expounding Ruth 4:16-22, the naming of Obed and the genealogy to David, showing how this small story fits God's grand plan that leads to Christ. A faithful, orthodox handling of this movement's climax and the book's purpose.

quiz.q: Who is credited with enabling Ruth to conceive?

options.text: The LORD, who is openly praised as the giver of the child.
options.note: Ruth 4:13 says the LORD enabled her to conceive, naming God's hand at the climax.

options.text: Boaz, through his own strength.
options.note: Boaz is the husband, but the text credits the conception to the LORD.

options.text: Naomi, through her careful planning.
options.note: Naomi planned wisely, but Scripture gives the credit to God, not to her scheming.

options.text: The elders at the gate.
options.note: The elders blessed the marriage, but God is named as the one who gave the child.

quiz.q: What did the women of Bethlehem call the newborn child?

options.text: A kinsman-redeemer for Naomi, who would renew her life.
options.note: Ruth 4:14-15 calls the child Naomi's redeemer, filling her emptiness.

options.text: A burden that Naomi was too old to raise.
options.note: The child is celebrated as a blessing and redeemer, not a burden.

options.text: A replacement for Ruth in Naomi's affection.
options.note: The child renews Naomi, and Ruth is praised as better than seven sons, not replaced.

options.text: A child with no importance to the family line.
options.note: The child is central; he leads to David and the Messiah.

quiz.q: How is Ruth described in the women's blessing?

options.text: As one who loves Naomi and is better to her than seven sons.
options.note: Ruth 4:15 gives Ruth this striking praise, answering Naomi's earlier emptiness.

options.text: As a foreigner who could never truly belong.
options.note: The opposite: she is honored above seven sons and placed in the Messiah's line.

options.text: As a burden Naomi had to tolerate.
options.note: Ruth is celebrated as a loving daughter-in-law, not tolerated.

options.text: As someone who had failed Naomi.
options.note: Ruth is praised for her love and loyalty, not blamed for failure.

quiz.q: What does the closing genealogy reveal?

options.text: That the child Obed is the grandfather of King David, so the whole story was preparing the royal line.
options.note: Ruth 4:17-22 ends on David, disclosing the book's larger purpose.

options.text: That the family faded into obscurity.
options.note: The opposite: the line leads to David and, ultimately, to Christ.

options.text: That the story has no connection to the rest of the Bible.
options.note: The genealogy deliberately ties Ruth into the line of promise and the wider canon.

options.text: That Boaz was unrelated to David.
options.note: Boaz is David's great-grandfather in this very genealogy.

quiz.q: How does the end of Ruth point to Jesus?

options.text: The line leads to David, and from David comes Jesus, the Son of David, born in Bethlehem.
options.note: Matthew 1 completes the line from Boaz and Ruth to Christ.

options.text: It points only to David and stops there with no further meaning.
options.note: David is the immediate goal, but the New Testament carries the line to Jesus.

options.text: It shows that redemption was only ever about land.
options.note: The land redemption serves a larger purpose: preserving the line that leads to the Redeemer.

options.text: It has nothing to do with the coming Messiah.
options.note: The genealogy is exactly how Ruth connects to the Messiah in Matthew 1.

questions: Naomi went out full, came back empty, and now holds a grandson on her lap. Where do you long for God to fill an emptiness in your life, and how does Naomi's story build your hope?
The LORD, hidden through most of the book, is openly praised at the end. Looking back over a hard season, where can you now see God's faithful hand at work?
Ruth's quiet loyalty turned out to be a vital link in God's great plan. How does this encourage you that your ordinary faithfulness matters more than you can see?
A Moabite outsider became the great-grandmother of David and an ancestor of Jesus. How does God's welcome of outsiders shape your view of your own belonging in His family?
The whole story leads to Bethlehem and to Christ the Redeemer. How does seeing Jesus at the end of Ruth deepen your worship of Him as your Redeemer?

translationNotes.note: Kinsman-redeemer renders goel; strikingly it is applied to the newborn child, who secures Naomi's line and future, the BSB footnote pointing to the legal role of Leviticus 25.
Better to you than seven sons is the highest praise in a culture that prized sons; it answers Naomi's cry of emptiness in chapter one.
Obed means one who serves or worships; the neighbor women name him, and the verse leaps ahead to David, the goal of the whole book.
These are the generations renders the toledot formula that structures Genesis, tying Ruth into the line of promise; the same names appear in Matthew 1.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Ruth 4:13-22. Verse 20 follows the BSB reading Salmon, noted in the source with manuscript variants (Salma).
